article.title: Is It “Miss You” or “Missing You”? Both Are Correct
article.excerpt: Both are correct. “I miss you” is the simple present and the default; “I’m missing you” is the progressive, which standard English avoids with a state verb and Indian English treats as entirely normal. “I missed you” is a different question.

keyTakeaways: Both forms are correct: “I miss you” is the unmarked simple present and “I’m missing you” the progressive, which runs about 52 times rarer in the Google Books English 2019 corpus.
“I am missing you” is not an error in Indian English — eWAVE 3.0 rates the progressive with stative verbs as pervasive or obligatory there, one of only 13 varieties out of 77.
The progressive means different things by variety: a temporary state in British and American English, an on-going state of extended duration in Indian English (van Rooy, 2014).
“I missed you” is past tense and a different question — it says the absence is over, so it is the wrong form to send while you are still apart.
Wording matters less than what surrounds it: the median miss-you letter on SubhSandesh is 88 words, and 43.5% of senders password-protect the page against 38.5% platform-wide.

faqs.question: Is it correct to say “I am missing you”?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is the present progressive of a state verb, which standard British and American English uses sparingly, so it reads as marked rather than wrong. In Indian English it is fully idiomatic: eWAVE 3.0 rates the extension of the progressive to stative verbs as pervasive or obligatory there, one of only 13 of the 77 varieties rated that way.

faqs.question: Which should I text, “I miss you” or “I’m missing you”?
faqs.answer: Send “I miss you” if you want the plain, unarguable version. Send “I’m missing you” if you want it to sound like right now rather than always — a particular evening, a particular week. Neither is a mistake, and in the Google Books English 2019 corpus the first is roughly 52 times more frequent than the two progressive forms combined.

faqs.question: Why does “I’m missing you” sound more intense?
faqs.answer: Because the progressive is doing no aspectual work. Missing someone is already a continuous state, so marking it as in progress adds nothing grammatically and readers take the extra marking as emphasis. Granath and Wherrity’s 2013 study argues that is exactly what the -ing form does with so-called stative verbs — it carries expressive rather than aspectual meaning.

faqs.question: Is “I am missing you” wrong in Indian English?
faqs.answer: No, and telling an Indian English speaker it is wrong is itself the error. The wider use of the progressive with state verbs is a documented feature of the variety, catalogued as eWAVE feature 88 and rated pervasive or obligatory for Indian English. Salles-Bernal’s 2015 corpus study also found Indian English had the highest progressive frequency of the three Asian varieties compared.

faqs.question: What is the difference between “I miss you” and “I missed you”?
faqs.answer: Tense, not tone. “I miss you” is present and true while you are apart; “I missed you” is past and says the absence has ended, which is what you say at the airport or on the call after a trip. Sending the past tense while you are still apart implies the missing has stopped.

faqs.question: Can I just write “Missing you” on its own?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is an elliptical form with the subject and auxiliary dropped, the same way “See you soon” drops “I’ll”. It reads as lighter and less committal than the full sentence, which suits a caption or a short message better than a letter.

faqs.question: Is “miss” a stative verb?
faqs.answer: In the emotional sense, yes. The Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English defines it as “to feel sad because someone you love is not with you” — a state of feeling, alongside know, believe, love and want. Its other senses, such as failing to hit something or lacking something, behave more dynamically, which is why “I’m missing a page” sounds completely ordinary.

faqs.question: Should I say “I miss talking to you” or “I miss to talk to you”?
faqs.answer: “I miss talking to you.” Miss takes an -ing form, never an infinitive, and the dictionaries flag this explicitly as a usage trap. The same applies to “I miss seeing you” and “I miss hearing your voice.”

faqs.question: Does “I’m missing you” mean something different to a British reader?
faqs.answer: Slightly. Van Rooy’s 2014 study found the Inner Circle prototype for a stative progressive is a temporary state, while Indian, Kenyan and Black South African English use it for an on-going state of extended duration. So a British or American reader may hear “this week” where an Indian English speaker means “all the time”.

faqs.question: How common is “I am missing you” compared with “I miss you”?
faqs.answer: In the Google Books English 2019 corpus, checked on 2026-09-25, “I miss you” runs at about 1.02 per million n-grams, “I’m missing you” at 0.011 and “I am missing you” at 0.008 — a gap of roughly 52 to 1. That is written, edited prose, the register where the progressive is rarest, so it overstates the gap in speech and messaging.

faqs.question: Could “I’m missing you” be misread?
faqs.answer: In a formal context, yes. Miss also means absent or lacking, and in the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank every one of the ten -ing tokens of the verb carries that sense — “I am missing Deal No. 74419 on your sheet”. In a personal message the emotional reading is obvious, so the risk is confined to work email and formal notes.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Is It "Miss You" or "Missing You"? Both Are Correct

Is it miss you or missing you? Both are correct English and they are not interchangeable. "I miss you" is the simple present and the default. "I'm missing you" is the progressive, which standard English usually avoids with a state verb, so it reads as marked — warmer, more spoken, tied to right now.

In Indian English it is not marked at all: that is a documented feature, not an error. "I missed you" is a separate question — past tense.

The hesitation is real and it costs time. Across 214 SubhSandesh miss-you pages, the median gap from first save to last edit is 2.6 hours, and 88.8% of started pages are published and shared — roughly one in nine is written and never sent.

## Both forms are correct — the difference is aspect, not right and wrong

Neither is a mistake. "I miss you" and "I'm missing you" differ in **aspect**: the simple present states a condition, the progressive frames it as in progress.

With most verbs that is obvious: "I eat" is a habit, "I'm eating" is happening now. With *miss* the contrast is subtler, because missing someone is already a continuous state — the progressive has nothing new to mark, so readers take the extra marking as emphasis.

That is why "I'm missing you" lands as more immediate and more temporary, even though neither form is more true. [Rautionaho's 2020 paper](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/weng.12520) in *World Englishes* found that studies making the standard claim about these forms often fail to control for how varieties differ, so treat anyone who calls one of them simply wrong with suspicion.

## "Miss" is a state verb, and that is the whole explanation

Grammars split English verbs into dynamic verbs (run, build, write) and stative verbs — verbs of feeling and cognition such as *know*, *believe*, *love*, *want* and, in its emotional sense, *miss*. The Longman Dictionary of Contemporary English defines that sense as "to feel sad because someone you love is not with you": a state, not an activity.

The textbook rule is that stative verbs resist the progressive. A [2023 corpus study](https://doaj.org/article/8874a46284eb48dbbc029c505630549b) in *Linguistics* tested it against native data from COCA and found progressive *-ing* strongly associated with activity verbs, with **stative verbs least likely of all to be inflected with the progressive**.

So "I'm missing you" breaks a soft statistical tendency, not a hard rule. [Granath and Wherrity's 2013 study](https://doaj.org/article/9a0d822499324bf18382f2dc2f1f30ab) argues every so-called stative verb can take the progressive, and that these forms are labelled odd mainly because they belong to *spoken* English while most grammar descriptions were built on written English. Their evidence is 132 tokens of *be loving* and 66 of *be knowing* in the Corpus of Historical American English.

A text message is spoken English typed out. That, not a rule, is why "I'm missing you" reads fine in a message and stiff in an essay.

## Miss you vs missing you vs missed you: the comparison

I measured the four forms in the Google Books Ngram Viewer (English 2019 corpus, no smoothing, checked 2026-09-25), in occurrences per million n-grams of matching length. Two caveats: books are edited prose, so these numbers understate the spoken forms, and "I miss you" is a three-word string measured against four-word ones, so the ratios are close rather than exact.

| Form | Grammatical status | Relative frequency, Google Books English 2019 | What it implies | Where it fits on a miss-you page (n=214, median letter 88 words) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I miss you | Simple present, unmarked | 1.02 per million — the baseline | A standing condition, no time limit | The opening line; safe anywhere in an 88-word letter |
| I'm missing you | Present progressive, marked in standard English | 0.011 per million — about 1/90th of "I miss you" | Right now, this stretch, this evening | Mid-letter, or in one of the 3.2 "open when" letters the average page carries |
| I am missing you | Progressive, uncontracted | 0.008 per million — the rarest of the four | Same as above, more formal or more Indian-English | A voice note, which 13.6% of senders record |
| I missed you | Simple past | 0.83 per million — nearly as common as "I miss you" | A finished stretch of absence, usually already over | After a reunion date lands; 28.0% of pages set one |

"I miss you" outnumbers both progressive forms put together by roughly **52 to 1** there, and beats "I missed you" by only about 1.2 to 1. That is the practical answer: the progressive is the unusual choice, the past tense is not.

## In Indian English, "I am missing you" is a documented feature, not an error

If you grew up speaking Indian English, "I am missing you" probably sounds normal — and the reference works say it should.

The *electronic World Atlas of Varieties of English* ([eWAVE 3.0](https://ewave-atlas.org/parameters/88)) catalogues feature 88, "wider range of uses of progressive be + V-ing than in StE: extension to stative verbs". Of the 77 varieties rated on it, 13 score **A — "feature is pervasive or obligatory"**, and Indian English is one of them.

Colloquial American English scores B. eWAVE's illustrative Indian English example is *We are knowing each other*.

Corpus work agrees on direction. [Salles-Bernal's 2015 study](https://doaj.org/article/08247077c7804f19b78aebe7fc612434) of the International Corpus of English found Indian English had the highest frequency of the progressive of the three Asian varieties compared — ahead of Singapore and Hong Kong English — and that the progressive is more frequent in speech than in writing in every variety examined.

[Van Rooy's 2014 study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/weng.12079) explains the feel of it. Comparing Indian, Kenyan and Black South African English, he found all three use the progressive proportionally more often with stative verbs than British English does, and that their prototype is an **on-going state of extended duration** — where the Inner Circle prototype is a *temporary* state.

That is the real difference, and none of the five top-ranking pages I read for this search mentions it — none of them uses the word *stative* either. From a British or American speaker, "I'm missing you" implies *this week, this trip*.

In Indian English it implies no time limit at all. The same five words carry two different promises.

One correction, because it is usually overstated: Rautionaho's 2020 re-analysis found that once you control for regional differences in verb-phrase density, the claim that Outer Circle varieties simply use stative progressives *more often* is **not confirmed** — though Indian English still came out different from the other varieties tested. The safe statement is that the form is idiomatic in Indian English, not that Indians say it more.

## "I missed you" is a different question

Three of the top five pages for this search answer *miss vs missed* instead, which is a separate confusion worth clearing up.

"I missed you" is past tense: a stretch of absence that has ended — the airport, the door, the call after the trip. Said while you are still apart, it implies the missing has stopped, which is almost never what the sender means.

"I miss you" is the one for a message sent across distance. On SubhSandesh, 28.0% of miss-you senders set a reunion countdown: before that date the present tense is the accurate one, and after it the past tense finally becomes true.

One more trap the dictionaries flag: *miss* takes an *-ing* form, never an infinitive. "I miss seeing you every day" is correct; "I miss to see you every day" is not.

## "Missing" has a second meaning, and it can misfire

*Miss* has more senses than the emotional one, and the progressive belongs more naturally to the others.

I checked the verb in the Universal Dependencies English Web Treebank — real American web text: emails, reviews, blog posts, forum threads. The lemma *miss* appears ten times as an *-ing* form across its three splits, and **every one is the "absent" or "lacking" sense**: "I am missing Deal No. 74419 on your sheet", "maybe I'm missing something here", "a nail missing".

Not one is the emotional sense. Ten tokens proves nothing about how rare the emotional progressive is, but it shows which reading written English trains people to reach for first — a reason to keep the progressive for messages where the emotional frame is already obvious.

## What actually changes the message

Choosing between two forms of two words is the smallest lever you have. The median miss-you letter on SubhSandesh is 88 words, the longest 1,024, so the opening you pick moves about 3% of an average letter.

What sits around it moves more. Miss-you senders are the most private segment measured on the platform: 43.5% password-protect the page before sharing it, against 38.5% across all 5,199 pages. These messages are written for exactly one reader — which is also why the form can be as informal as you like.

If the whole message is that one line, the [I-miss-you page for a partner](/missyou-gf) gives it somewhere to land: a letter, memories and a countdown rather than a notification that scrolls away. If it is genuinely a letter and you would rather it arrive line by line, [Catch](/catch) drops one line at a time and suits a long note better. For anything not romantic — a sibling, a friend, a parent — start from the [full template list](/templates), because a page built for a partner reads wrong sent to a brother.

Once the form is settled, the wording around it is the harder problem, and [what to say when you miss someone](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/what-to-say-when-you-miss-someone) covers that rather than this grammar question.

One disclosure belongs with those numbers: the database records which template was opened, never who received it or what was written in it.

## Where this answer runs out

Two limits worth stating plainly.

First, the first-party numbers cover 214 pages over two months — the template went live on 2026-07-28 — so nothing here supports a seasonal claim, and the sample is too small to split by region.

Second, none of the corpora here is a corpus of Indian text messages. eWAVE records specialist judgement; the ICE and COHA studies cover published and interview data; Google Books is edited prose.

The register you are writing in — a private message between two people — is the least documented English there is. For what your own reader expects, the better evidence is the last twenty messages the two of you sent.

If you still cannot decide, send "I miss you". It is the unmarked form, it is correct in every variety of English, and it is the one nobody will read twice.

structuralLimitations: BRIEF FRAMING VERIFIED AND PARTLY CORRECTED. The task prompt asserted that “I am missing you” is “markedly more common” in Indian English than in US/UK English. The atlas rating supports the feature being pervasive (eWAVE 3.0 feature 88, Indian English = A), but Rautionaho 2020 (World Englishes) found that once regional differences in verb-phrase density are accounted for, the claim that Outer Circle varieties make MORE FREQUENT use of stative progressives is NOT confirmed — though Indian English came out different from Singapore and Hong Kong English. The post therefore says the form is idiomatic and unmarked in Indian English, and explicitly declines to say Indians use it more often. Van Rooy 2014 is the load-bearing claim instead: the Outer Circle prototype is an on-going state of extended duration, against the Inner Circle’s temporary state.
The prompt’s framing that the progressive reads as “more temporary” is supported for British/American English by van Rooy 2014 and is stated that way in the post, not as a universal.

ABSTRACT-ONLY READS: van Rooy 2014 and Rautionaho 2020, both World Englishes (Wiley). onlinelibrary.wiley.com returns HTTP 403 to this environment; both abstracts were read in full from the publisher’s Crossref deposit (api.crossref.org/works/<doi>), and nothing beyond the abstract is claimed. Both are named in the body so a reader can rerun them; neither is counted in batchMeta.sources. Caveat stated in the body: “I miss you” is a 3-gram compared against 4-grams, so the 52:1 ratio is approximate.

CANNIBALISATION: 81 live slugs contain ‘miss’ and none is a grammar or usage post — they are message/quote/shayari lists and page-builder tools. auditReport.honestAssessment: The five pages I read from this SERP (oneminuteenglish, lovelingolab, textranch x2, attractiondiary; 537-1,471 words) all answer the question from intuition. Not one uses the word stative, names a corpus, cites a dictionary or mentions Indian English at all, and three of them answer miss vs missed instead of miss vs missing. This post gives the mechanism (miss is a state verb, so the progressive carries expressive rather than aspectual meaning), a reproducible frequency measurement, and the finding that actually matters to an Indian reader: the progressive is pervasive in Indian English per eWAVE 3.0 and means an on-going rather than a temporary state per van Rooy 2014. It also states the correction most sources get wrong, that Rautionaho 2020 did not confirm higher Outer Circle frequency once verb-phrase density is controlled. That combination is genuinely absent from the SERP and is the reason an answer engine would have something to cite here. Against that: textranch and english.stackexchange carry far more domain authority and topical history on usage queries, subhsandesh.in has none in the grammar space, and this is the only grammar post on a domain of gifting and message content, so it has no internal cluster to lean on. Ranking would take months if it happens at all, and the first-party data, while unique, is only tangential to a grammar question - it supports the wording-matters-less-than-context section, not the linguistics.
